description: Hello, my name's Bishal! I am a solo team who likes dealing with security systems and working on datasets to help me out as well.
summary: Vital Orbit Pulse is health monitoring software for astronauts on a Mars transit, where a signal takes 3 to 22 minutes to reach Earth. It answers the challenge by guiding the crew at once, with no round trip to ground control. Each astronaut has a Durable Object that runs a playbook of health rules against live readings and personal baselines, and pushes guidance and checklists to the crew immediately. Earth receives the same data only after the real light delay, using Durable Object alarms. NASA DONKI space weather events can trigger the rules. Every decision is written to a hash-chained black box in R2 with Bucket Lock, so records cannot be edited or deleted, even by us. Tiger Data keeps months of history for trends. This matters because on a long mission the crew must act on their own, and Earth still needs a record it can trust.
details:
What it does and how it works
Vital Orbit Pulse is a crew health monitoring web app for a Mars transit. Sensor readings enter through a Worker and a Queue and reach one Durable Object per astronaut. That object runs a playbook of health rules against personal baselines and pushes guidance and action checklists to the crew over a WebSocket at once. It also sets an alarm for the real Earth to Mars light delay, and only when the alarm fires does mission control see the same data. A critical alert starts a Workflow that notifies the crew, waits for the shelter checklist with a timeout, and pages the commander if the timeout hits. A twin forecast projects each trend forward. An AI flight surgeon explains readings from the playbook, and it explains but does not diagnose. NASA DONKI space weather events can trigger playbook rules.

Benefits and intended impact
On a long mission the crew cannot wait minutes for ground control, so they get guidance at the edge. Earth still receives a full record, and every decision is written to a hash-chained black box stored in R2 with Bucket Lock. Records cannot be overwritten or deleted, so a review after an incident can trust what it reads. Crew also choose what the flight surgeon can see.

Tools, languages and software

  • Languages: Python (the main Worker) and TypeScript (a small database Worker and the React frontend).
  • Cloudflare: Workers, Durable Objects and alarms, Queues, Workflows, D1, R2 with Bucket Lock, Workers AI, AI Gateway, Vectorize, Hyperdrive, Cron Triggers, Cloudflare Access, and service bindings.
  • Tiger Data: a TimescaleDB hypertable of every reading, with time_bucket daily averages for trend charts and a 90-day baseline for each astronaut.
  • Auth0: sign-in behind Cloudflare Access, with a role claim for crew and mission control.
  • Data: NASA DONKI.
  • Hardware: none. A crew simulator feeds the readings. [Edit this if you used real sensors.]

How it is creative
We made the light delay a real mechanism and not an animation: a Durable Object alarm holds each message until the delay passes, so mission control sees only what it could really see. The black box can show itself being tampered with: R2 refuses the edit on the real copy, and a hash check catches the edit on a demo copy. Playbooks are swappable, so the same app can run a Mars transit or a low Earth orbit station with different autonomy and delay. The Under the hood panel shows live system state to anyone who wants to check our claims.

Factors our team considered

  • Autonomy: the edge must be able to act when Earth cannot answer.
  • Trust: the record has to be one that nobody, including us, can edit.
  • Privacy: crew control what the flight surgeon sees.
  • Honesty about limits: Python Workers have no TCP sockets, so a TypeScript Worker owns the database. The Queue has no backlog API, so we show our own count.
  • Safety: the AI explains readings and never diagnoses.
